finding: Error labels exist for a small fraction of the audio
evidence: 3,599 of 26,867 scripted utterances (13.4%) plus 22 suitcase narratives are manually annotated; the rest have forced alignment only
implication: Supervised error-type training and evaluation use only the annotated subset (about 120k phone events); the other 87% of the audio is useful only for self-supervised or pseudo-label use. State this scope in the report.

finding: Phone-level error labels are skewed and the rare classes are very rare
evidence: correct = 84.5% of phone events; among errors: substitution 75.8%, addition only 5.9% (1,092); 4-class imbalance ratio 93:1
implication: Use class weights / focal loss or resampling and macro-F1 / per-class recall. Report additions and deletions separately from substitutions. Resampling must happen inside the training split only.

finding: Error profile depends strongly on L1 and on the individual speaker
evidence: error rate per 100 phones: Arabic 9.8, Hindi 14.0, Korean 9.4, Mandarin 15.4, Spanish 16.0, Vietnamese 23.4; deletion share of errors 10%-32%; speaker range 6.8-26.5
implication: Aggregate metrics will hide weak L1 groups; report every L2-ARCTIC result per L1 (and per speaker where useful). This is the data basis for the Sprint 8 generalisation story.

finding: Only 24 speakers (4 per L1): any speaker-independent split is statistically thin
evidence: 24 speakers; 4 per L1 (2 F + 2 M); annotated utterances per speaker 149-150
implication: A single fixed test set of a few speakers gives high-variance estimates. Prefer grouped (speaker-held-out) cross-validation, stratified by L1 and gender, or hold out 1 speaker per L1 for test with 1 per L1 for validation. Save speaker lists per fold for audit.

finding: Completeness score is degenerate
evidence: completeness = 10 for 99.5% of utterances; only 25 of 5,000 are below 10
implication: Do not model completeness: it is not one of the six heads in the proposal. Keep the column in the manifests for reference.

finding: Word stress is almost always correct and expert agreement is weak
evidence: 0.90% of words have stress = 5 (287 of 31,816); pairwise r = 0.19, ICC(2,1) = 0.13
implication: Not one of the six proposed heads, so leave it out of modeling. If it is ever used, treat it as rare-event detection with balanced metrics and expect a very low ceiling.

finding: Phone-level labels are heavily skewed toward 'correct'
evidence: 92.1% of expert labels are 2; consensus score < 0.5 for 3.6% of tokens, < 1.0 for 4.8%; imbalance ratio 20:1 (binary at 1.0)
implication: Use weighted loss or resampling and report per-class / balanced metrics; fix and document the binarisation threshold before Sprint 3 (it changes prevalence from 3.6% to 19.3%). Keep phone scores as a regression target as well.

finding: Most score variance is between speakers
evidence: between-speaker share of variance: accuracy 70%, fluency 76%, prosodic 78%, total 73%
implication: Splits must be speaker-independent (random utterance splits would leak speaker identity). Validation needs enough speakers (not utterances) to be stable: 125 train speakers, so a ~15% validation set is ~19 speakers.

finding: Label schemes do not overlap: scores vs categorical error tags
evidence: SpeechOcean762 has sentence/word/phoneme scores; L2-ARCTIC has phone-level error types only (no sentence or word scores)
implication: Model each dataset with its own heads. Multi-task learning (Sprint 6) can share an encoder across datasets but not a joint label set; plan the 6-head scope around this (Sprint 7 scope review).

finding: Suitcase (spontaneous) subset is a different domain and very small
evidence: 22 narratives, 26.1 minutes; error rate 21.7 vs 14.7 per 100 phones in scripted speech; no forced-alignment TextGrid
implication: Keep it out of training and validation; use it only as an optional out-of-domain evaluation.

finding: Error support is uneven across phonemes
evidence: top-5 phonemes (Z, DH, R, D, AH) hold 43% of substitution + deletion events; 2 of 39 standard phonemes have < 50 error events (M, OY) and 9 have < 100; highest error rates: DH 54%, Z 51%, TH 44%, JH 42%
implication: Per-phoneme classifiers are not viable for the low-support phonemes; group phonemes (manner / place classes) for error-type tasks and show per-phoneme support next to every per-phoneme metric.

finding: Annotated prompts are shared across speakers, so text cannot be disjoint under a speaker split
evidence: 300 distinct annotated prompts; 99 annotated for all 24 speakers; 119 annotated only for one L1's 4 speakers (L1-targeted sentences) and 100 covering all six L1s
implication: Speaker-independent splits will repeat sentence text across partitions; acceptable for pronunciation assessment but state it. Do not stratify by prompt.

finding: Annotation tags are inconsistently formatted and contain typos
evidence: 9,105 of 20,829 error tags contain stray whitespace; 182 use upper-case s/d/a; 6 canonical labels are typos (D_, ER), V``, W`, Y_, Z_); 3,675 empty phone intervals
implication: Always read tags through `parse_phone_label`; in US 2.2 add an explicit mapping of the typo labels to the 39-phone inventory and a validation step that fails on unknown symbols.

finding: Policy decisions needed for 'err' and '*' perceived tags
evidence: 262 substitutions are tagged 'err' (sound not identified) and 1,744 carry '*' (accented variant of the phone)
implication: Decide and document: treat '*' as an error (accented deviation) or as correct-with-accent, and map 'err' to a generic substitution class. The choice changes scripted substitution counts by about 10% (1,471 of 14,098), concentrated in Arabic and Hindi speakers (mostly R to R* and T to T*). Keep an `is_deviation` flag so results can be reported both ways.

finding: Utterance-level 'has an error' label is almost always positive
evidence: 96.4% of annotated utterances contain at least one error; mean 5.2 error events per utterance
implication: Do not use binary utterance-level error detection as a target; use error rate / count regression. Word-level 'has error' is far more balanced and is a reasonable derived target.

finding: Error-type information is thin and mostly 'deleted' or 'unrecognisable'
evidence: only 3,403 phone tokens (3.6%) carry a pronounced-phone label; 846 are <DEL> and 820 are <unk>
implication: Use L2-ARCTIC (not SpeechOcean762) for error-type classification; SpeechOcean762 supports scoring tasks only.

finding: Single native language
evidence: all 250 speakers are Mandarin L1 (per the corpus README)
implication: Generalisation across L1 backgrounds cannot be tested on this dataset; that question depends on L2-ARCTIC (Sprint 8).

finding: A few phonemes have very few tokens
evidence: 2 phonemes with < 100 tokens: ZH (n=25), OY (n=56)
implication: Exclude from per-phoneme breakdowns (or pool) and avoid reading per-phoneme metrics for them.

finding: Sentence and word scores are left-skewed; extremes are rare
evidence: modal sentence 'total' score is 8 (37% of utterances); accuracy <= 3 for 183 utterances; 88.8% of words score 10, 9.0% score <= 6
implication: Prefer regression with MAE/RMSE/PCC; do not treat the 0-10 scale as 11 classes. Add error-by-score-band reporting so low-score failures are visible (Sprint 3 weakness diagnosis).

finding: Human agreement bounds attainable performance
evidence: sentence pairwise r = 0.66-0.71; leave-one-out r = 0.77-0.80; phone Fleiss kappa = 0.46; consensus accuracy/fluency/prosodic equal the median of the 5 experts in 100% of utterances
implication: Interpret model correlations relative to the leave-one-out ceiling, and report the same agreement figures in the final report as label-noise context.

finding: Children and adults differ in prompt length, speaking rate and score spread
evidence: mean words per utterance: child/teen 5.6 vs adult 7.1; phones per second: 4.77 vs 5.22; speaker-mean total score std: child/teen 0.74 vs adult 1.74
implication: A model can use age or prompt-length cues as shortcuts; evaluate within each age group and consider length-matched sanity checks.

finding: Phoneme symbols need unification
evidence: SpeechOcean762 uses 39 ARPAbet base phones with stress digits; L2-ARCTIC canonical labels contain 46 symbols (7 non-standard: AX and typo labels); phoneme-difficulty agreement for Mandarin speakers: Spearman rho = 0.50 over 36 phonemes
implication: Map both to a common 39-phone inventory (stress kept as a separate feature) in US 2.2. A moderate rho means phoneme difficulty transfers only partly between the corpora.

finding: Different speaker populations
evidence: SpeechOcean762: 122 child/teen + 128 adult Mandarin speakers; L2-ARCTIC: 24 adults across 6 L1s
implication: Cross-dataset conclusions mix age, L1 and recording conditions; avoid attributing differences to a single factor.

finding: Sampling rate and a few audio irregularities
evidence: all audio is 44.1 kHz mono (SpeechOcean762 is 16 kHz); 41 scripted clips < 1 s; SKA has 974 and EBVS 1007 utterances (others ~1,130)
implication: Resample to 16 kHz in US 2.2 for compatibility with the pretrained encoders and SpeechOcean762. Uneven per-speaker counts are harmless for the annotated subset (149-150 each).

finding: Small numbers of segments outside word boundaries or very short
evidence: 120 addition intervals and 7 correct phones fall outside any word interval; 194 speech phones are shorter than 20 ms
implication: Check these during the US 2.2 alignment validation; additions between words need an explicit attachment rule (e.g. to the following word).

finding: A small amount of prompt text is shared between train and test
evidence: 52 test utterances (2.1%) have a prompt that also occurs in train; 4,947 distinct prompts for 5,000 utterances
implication: Negligible leakage risk; note it in the report. No text-disjoint split is required for this dataset.

finding: A few long clips; audio format is uniform
evidence: longest clip 20.4 s (train) vs 12.2 s in test; 9 clips > 15 s from 4 speakers (age groups: adult); all audio is already 16 kHz mono 16-bit
implication: Set a max length for batching (about 20.5 s covers everything); no resampling needed for this dataset.

finding: Train and test differ slightly by age group, but not significantly
evidence: speaker-mean total score: adults train 6.72 vs test 7.04 (Mann-Whitney p = 0.26); child/teen train 7.72 vs test 7.48 (p = 0.27); utterance-level KS p-values for the four main scores: 0.05-0.58
implication: Keep the official test set untouched. The differences are small next to the between-speaker variance (SO-8) and not significant with ~60 speakers per group, but report child/teen and adult results separately and stratify the validation split by age group.
